short: In January 27 BCE Octavian returned formal authority to the Senate and received it back as command, provinces, and the name Augustus.
full:
On 13 January 27 BCE, Octavian appeared before the Senate and formally laid down the extraordinary powers he had held since the civil wars, restoring the res publica in name. Three days later the Senate granted him back a ten-year proconsular command over Gaul, Spain, Syria, Cilicia, Cyprus and Egypt, provinces holding most of Rome's twenty-eight legions, together with the honorific title Augustus.

The remaining provinces kept proconsuls chosen by lot, but Augustus's legates now governed wherever the army mattered, and only he held a command renewed by the Senate every decade thereafter. The settlement gave the new order a constitutional face: Augustus was princeps, first citizen, not king or dictator, while holding military power no rival could match. Refined again in 23 BCE, the arrangement became the template later emperors inherited.
